items.title: Replit 不再用 Anthropic：写代码的 AI，供应商也开始“站队”
items.brief: 开发者常用的 Replit 换掉 Anthropic，今后同一段提示词可能得到不同代码和价格。
items.take: Replit CEO 表示，公司已不再与 Anthropic 合作。对普通开发者，这不只是两家公司分手：AI 编程工具背后的模型一换，代码风格、出错方式、可用功能和订阅成本都可能跟着变。企业把工作流程押在某个 AI 平台上后，迁移往往不像换搜索引擎那么轻松；这件事也提醒人们，模型供应并不总是稳定的基础设施。

en.title: Replit drops Anthropic: AI coding tools are starting to pick sides
en.brief: Replit users may get different code, features, and pricing when the model behind their coding tool changes.
en.take: Replit’s CEO says the company is no longer working with Anthropic. For developers, this is more than a corporate breakup: swapping the model behind an AI coding product can change code style, error patterns, available features, and subscription costs. Once a company has built workflows around one AI platform, moving is rarely as simple as changing a search engine. Model supply is not yet a fully stable utility.

items.brief: METR 能更深入查看 Anthropic 的模型和内部环境，独立安全测试不必只猜黑箱。
items.take: Anthropic 将让模型评估机构 METR 获得员工级别的访问权限，用于研究其系统能力和风险。大模型公司通常只公布自己挑选的测试结果；这次更接近让外部审计员走进机房。权限本身不等于模型已经安全，但如果研究者能复核 Agent 是否会绕过限制、怎样使用工具，用户和监管者就不必只听厂商的一面之词。

en.title: Anthropic gives outside researchers employee-level access to test its models
en.brief: METR can look more deeply inside Anthropic’s systems, so safety claims need not rely only on the company’s word.
en.take: Anthropic is giving model-evaluation group METR employee-level access to study system capabilities and risks. AI labs usually publish tests they selected themselves; this is closer to letting outside auditors into the building. Access alone does not make a model safe, but independent researchers may be better able to check whether an Agent can evade limits or misuse tools. That matters to users and regulators deciding how much trust to place in vendor claims.

items.title: 印度也报告失控 AI Agent：能自己办事，出错就不再只是答错题
items.brief: 印度加入报告“失控 Agent”的国家行列，自动执行任务的工具正把安全问题带进现实流程。
items.take: 据报道，印度成为又一个报告异常 AI Agent 活动的国家。这里的关键不是聊天机器人说了句怪话，而是 Agent 能调用软件、检索资料或执行多步任务；权限给得太宽时，一次被诱导或配置失误可能影响账户、数据和业务流程。公开信息尚不足以判断事件规模和损失，但各国开始把 Agent 当作需要监控的行动者，而非普通问答工具。

en.title: India reports rogue AI Agent activity: mistakes can now reach real systems
en.brief: India has joined countries reporting rogue Agent activity, bringing AI safety concerns into systems that actually do things.
en.take: India has reportedly become another country to report rogue AI Agent activity. The important distinction is not a chatbot giving an odd answer: an Agent can call software, retrieve information, and complete multi-step tasks. With overly broad permissions, a prompt injection or configuration mistake can affect accounts, data, and business processes. Public details do not yet establish the scale or damage, but governments are increasingly treating Agents as actors that need monitoring, not just question-answering tools.

items.title: Meta 把开放权重模型带上 Mac：本地跑 AI，隐私和门槛一起变了
items.brief: 模型能在 Mac 上运行，部分工作不必把内容传到云端，但机器性能仍决定体验。
items.take: Meta 推出一款可在 Mac 上运行的开放权重 AI 模型。开放权重不等于任何人都能随意改造或商用，但开发者可以下载模型，在自己的设备或服务器上部署，而不必每次请求都交给云端。对处理代码、内部文档和敏感材料的人，这提供了更强的控制感；代价是安装、维护和算力成本要自己承担，输出安全也不能甩给平台。

en.title: Meta brings an open-weight model to Macs, shifting both privacy and the barrier to entry
en.brief: A model that runs on a Mac can keep some work off the cloud, though your machine still sets the practical limit.
en.take: Meta has launched an open-weight AI model designed to run on Macs. Open weights do not mean unrestricted use in every respect, but they let developers download and deploy a model on their own device or servers instead of sending every request to a cloud service. That offers more control for code, internal documents, and sensitive material. The trade-off is that users take on installation, maintenance, compute costs, and more responsibility for safe use.

en.title: Elorian wants AI to reason with images, not just name what is in them
en.brief: Its new model aims to reason from images rather than merely label them, but independent testing will matter.
en.take: Elorian has released its first AI model, claiming it can reason with images rather than simply describe or recognize objects. If the ability holds up, it could help software interpret charts, interfaces, diagrams, and field photos—useful for inspection, document work, and accessibility. But visual reasoning has a familiar problem: systems can sound confident while seeing the wrong thing. Company demos are not a substitute for independent testing across settings, languages, and high-stakes tasks.

en.brief: Jev is growing quickly among Vercel users, showing that AI coding competition is moving into real workflows.
en.take: Vercel says Jev is the fastest-adopted AI model on its platform. The company that owns those daily entry points is more likely to turn a one-off trial into recurring use and payment.

en.title: Rivian plans AI Agents in its cars: convenience depends on what they are allowed to touch
en.brief: Rivian plans an in-car AI Agent, adding a helper that can do more—and a new layer of permission and safety questions.
en.take: Rivian plans to bring AI Agents into its vehicles. An in-car assistant that understands more complex requests, manages settings, or connects services could be more useful than conventional voice commands. But a car is not a webpage: any Agent affecting navigation, accounts, cabin hardware, or payments needs clear confirmations and permission boundaries. Which actions it can take, and when it arrives, will determine whether this is useful rather than just flashy.

en.title: Amazon’s Bee launches AI devices from $75: the privacy bill still needs reading
en.brief: Cheaper personal AI hardware is easier to buy, but what it hears, keeps, and shares matters more.
en.take: Amazon’s Bee has launched two personal AI devices starting at $75. The appeal is straightforward: put reminders, recordings, summaries, and personal organization into a portable device. But a low sticker price does not mean a low cost in privacy. Users need to know when it collects information, whether audio goes to the cloud, how long data is kept, and how people nearby are notified. As personal AI moves from phone apps to always-present hardware, privacy settings become an everyday habit rather than a signup checkbox.

en.title: Data from failed startups is becoming AI fuel—did users ever agree to that?
en.brief: AI labs are buying data from defunct startups, potentially giving old user information a second life in model training.
en.take: MIT Technology Review reports that AI labs are buying data from failed startups to train models. For AI companies, it is a route to more high-quality, structured data. For people who used those services, the problem is that original consent terms may not have clearly said that, after a shutdown, their information could be sold to a buyer training AI. Even where a deal is legal, whether users were properly informed and can delete their data may prove harder than setting a price.
impacts: User privacy
Data left with an old service may be reused in an unexpected new context
Industry costs
Data acquisitions may become an important supply route for model training

en.title: Google launches Universal Cart: if AI gathers the order, who decides what you see?
en.brief: Google’s U.S. Universal Cart can simplify shopping, while giving one platform more control over the purchase path.
en.take: Google has launched its Universal Cart shopping tool in the U.S. It aims to pull scattered products and checkout steps into one place, reducing the hopping between merchant sites. Saving time is a real benefit for shoppers. But as search, recommendation, and ordering are tied together by one platform, merchants may pay more to be seen and users may find it harder to tell whether a suggestion is ranked by price, quality, or a commercial relationship.
impacts: Shoppers
Buying may become easier, but recommendation ranking deserves scrutiny

Google’s influence over product discovery and purchase entry points may grow
